paragraphs: A question about a changing fact cannot always be answered without knowing which time period matters. This paper introduces a question-answering dataset designed to test that dependence on time. Its motivation is that existing datasets contain too few time-sensitive questions to give a useful picture of a model’s temporal understanding and reasoning.

The authors build the dataset by extracting facts that change over time from WikiData and linking them to corresponding Wikipedia pages. Crowd workers then check and correct these initially noisy facts. The verified annotations become the basis for question-answer pairs, connecting the questions to information whose timing affects the correct answer.

The evaluation includes long-document question-answering systems such as BigBird and FiD. FiD performs best among the evaluated systems but reaches only 46% accuracy, compared with 87% for humans. The authors’ analysis also finds inconsistent temporal reasoning. These results make the dataset useful for studying whether systems can reason about temporal changes, beyond simply finding relevant text.
neurips-2021-a-dataset-for-answering-tim.tldr: A time-sensitive question-answering dataset exposes a substantial gap between tested language models and human temporal reasoning.

paragraphs: Measurements of individual cells can reveal their molecular state through chromatin accessibility, RNA expression, and proteins. These datasets can contain millions of cells and tens of thousands of features, many of them sparse. The paper addresses the challenge of learning biologically meaningful patterns from such measurements while separating those patterns from technical noise.

A central difficulty is the limited availability of biological ground truth. The authors use technologies that measure two molecular layers in the same cell to obtain paired observations. They compare this arrangement to language translation: a measurement in one modality has a corresponding measurement in another, providing a concrete basis for evaluating prediction across modalities.

The contribution combines three tasks for cross-modality prediction and integrated representations with a new human bone marrow dataset designed for benchmarking. An open-source framework supports centralized evaluation of submitted methods. Together, these resources provide a shared setting for comparing how algorithms predict complementary measurements and combine them into representations of cellular state.
neurips-2021-a-sandbox-for-prediction-an.tldr: Paired molecular measurements, a bone marrow dataset, and shared tasks support benchmarking prediction and integration across single-cell modalities.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification asks models to learn new classification tasks from very little labeled data. Transfer learning and meta-learning both address this goal, but their research communities often evaluate progress differently. This paper introduces VTAB+MD, a shared evaluation protocol intended to make comparisons across the two families more direct and informative.

The authors evaluate leading approaches on both Meta-Dataset, associated with meta-learning, and the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark, associated with transfer learning. In this comparison, Big Transfer methods outperform competing approaches on Meta-Dataset on average, even when trained only on ImageNet. Meta-learning methods trained and validated on Meta-Dataset struggle to compete on VTAB.

The results also qualify the benefits of scale: increasing scale does not improve Big Transfer performance on Meta-Dataset tasks that are highly outside its training distribution. The study therefore provides evidence about both the strengths and boundaries of the evaluated approaches. Its broader contribution is an evaluation setting that lets insights from the two communities be assessed together.
neurips-2021-a-unified-few-shot-classifi.tldr: VTAB+MD compares transfer and meta-learning together, finding strong average transfer performance alongside limits on unfamiliar tasks.

paragraphs: High performance on ordinary language-understanding tests does not establish that a model handles deliberately challenging text reliably. AdvGLUE addresses this issue with a benchmark spanning multiple GLUE tasks and different adversarial attacks. The authors apply 14 attack methods and use human validation to check the resulting examples and annotations.

That validation exposes a problem with the attacks themselves. Around 90% of generated examples either alter the original meaning or also mislead human annotators. Such examples complicate interpretation because an apparent model failure may involve an invalid or ambiguous test item. The authors therefore carefully filter the generated material to construct the benchmark.

All language models and robust training methods tested perform poorly on the curated AdvGLUE examples relative to their accuracy on ordinary inputs. This finding establishes a vulnerability among the evaluated systems while also showing why attack quality matters for measuring robustness. The benchmark supports research on both meaning-preserving attacks and models that remain reliable under those attacks.
neurips-2021-adversarial-glue-a-multi-ta.tldr: AdvGLUE uses human-filtered adversarial examples to reveal robustness weaknesses across tested language models and training methods.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning learns representations of graph data without requiring human annotations. Although recent methods had achieved promising results, the reasons for their success remained unclear. This paper studies the design choices inside these methods so researchers can better understand how individual components and their combinations affect performance.

The authors organize the approach around graph augmentations, contrasting modes, learning objectives, and strategies for choosing negative examples. They then run controlled experiments on benchmark tasks across several domains. Their empirical findings suggest that simple changes to graph topology that create sparse views can improve performance. They also recommend matching what the method contrasts to the level of detail required by the final task.

These recommendations are empirical guidance from the study. To make further investigation easier, the authors introduce PyGCL, a library with interchangeable contrastive-learning components, standardized evaluation, and experiment management. The combination of controlled comparisons and reusable software helps researchers examine design choices within a common framework and build on the reported findings.
neurips-2021-an-empirical-study-of-graph.tldr: Controlled experiments identify useful graph contrastive-learning design choices, accompanied by the modular PyGCL research library.

paragraphs: Methods for reducing bias in deep representation learning are difficult to compare when they are evaluated under different conditions. This paper creates a common benchmarking framework and tests fairness methods on both synthetic and real-world data. The aim is to understand how these approaches behave and identify settings in which they fail.

The authors train about 3,000 models across configurations that vary data imbalance and correlations between attributes. In their experiments, model bias increases as the data become more imbalanced or attributes become more correlated. They also find that the dominance of correlated sensitive features affects bias, showing that the structure of the data matters when interpreting mitigation results.

Another reported finding is that sensitive information remains in learned representations even after bias-mitigation algorithms are applied. This highlights a distinction between applying a mitigation method and removing sensitive information from the representation. The released dataset, challenging configurations, and common evaluation framework provide resources for examining these behaviors systematically across the evaluated methods.
neurips-2021-benchmarking-bias-mitigatio.tldr: A shared benchmark finds that data imbalance and attribute correlations challenge bias mitigation, while sensitive information persists in learned representations.

paragraphs: Video models must handle changes in image content and disruptions in how that content unfolds over time. This paper introduces Mini Kinetics-C and Mini SSV2-C to evaluate both kinds of corruption. The benchmarks address a gap left by robustness research focused mainly on still images.

The study compares established convolutional and Transformer-based models that process spatial and temporal information. In the reported experiments, Transformer-based modeling provides better corruption robustness than the convolutional alternatives. The authors also connect generalization ability with resistance to temporal corruptions and find that greater model capacity and computational cost accompany improved robustness, especially for temporal disturbances.

These findings suggest a potential tension between computational efficiency and robustness in the evaluated video models. The authors further find that interventions used for image tasks, including training with noise, may not work for spatial-temporal models. The benchmark therefore offers a way to evaluate video-specific robustness and examine whether design and training choices withstand both spatial and temporal degradation.
neurips-2021-benchmarking-the-robustness.tldr: Two video benchmarks reveal how model architecture, capacity, and training choices relate to robustness against spatial and temporal corruptions.

paragraphs: CCNLab provides a shared way to evaluate computational models of learning against observed experimental data. Its initial focus is classical conditioning, the study of how animals learn to predict rewards and punishments in their environment. This gives the framework a defined set of learning phenomena through which different computational accounts can be examined.

The framework expresses simulations of influential experiments through a common programming interface. It also includes tools for visualizing simulated outcomes and comparing them with empirical observations. Its collection covers representative experiments from several categories of phenomena, allowing researchers to examine a model across a broader range of conditioning behavior.

The design supports adding further experiments and aims to reduce the effort required to use the benchmark. Its contribution is therefore a reusable setting for developing and comparing models against shared evidence. The authors envision it as a way to bring computational theories of brain learning together and encourage interaction among neuroscience, psychology, and artificial intelligence.
neurips-2021-ccnlab-a-benchmarking-frame.tldr: CCNLab supplies shared simulations and comparison tools for evaluating computational learning models against classical-conditioning experiments.

paragraphs: Many chest X-ray models learn from labels describing an entire image or from unstructured reports. Those resources provide limited support for quantitatively evaluating where findings occur and how model explanations relate to anatomy. Chest ImaGenome addresses this gap by organizing annotations for 242,072 images into anatomy-centered scene graphs.

The authors generate local annotations automatically using rule-based processing of reports together with atlas-based detection of anatomical bounding boxes. A radiologist-developed ontology connects anatomical regions and their attributes within each graph. The dataset includes 1,256 combinations of relation annotations involving 29 anatomical locations, giving the image description an explicit structure tied to localized regions.

The resource also contains more than 670,000 localized comparisons across sequential examinations, recording improvement, worsening, or no change. A manually annotated reference set covers 500 unique patients. These components support studying image-level reasoning and combinations of image and text information, while the local structure directly addresses the shortage of anatomy-linked labels described by the authors.
neurips-2021-chest-imagenome-dataset-for.tldr: Chest ImaGenome structures chest X-ray findings and changes over time as localized, anatomy-centered scene graphs.

paragraphs: Using a paper as a search query leaves an important ambiguity: a reader might want similar objectives, methods, or results. CSFCube introduces an evaluation collection for searches that specify both an example paper and one of these aspects. The task asks retrieval systems to find relevant scientific papers along the particular dimension the reader chooses.

The collection contains 50 English query papers from computational linguistics and machine learning venues. Experts assess candidate papers with graded relevance scores, allowing different degrees of relevance to the requested aspect. The authors follow TREC guidelines for pooling candidates at depths of 100 or 250 and report high agreement among annotators.

Evaluated state-of-the-art models leave a significant performance gap on this task. That finding suggests that matching papers along a chosen rhetorical aspect remains challenging for the tested systems. By making the requested aspect explicit and supplying expert relevance judgments, CSFCube provides a concrete evaluation target for more focused scientific literature search.
neurips-2021-csfcube-a-test-collection-o.tldr: CSFCube evaluates scientific-paper search that targets similarity in objectives, methods, or results using an example paper.

paragraphs: Online controlled experiments help digital services measure the effects of changes. This paper examines the public datasets available for studying such experiments and organizes them into a survey and taxonomy. The review identifies a particular gap: data suitable for researching adaptive stopping, where accumulating evidence informs when an experiment should end.

To address that gap, the authors release daily snapshots of decision metrics from multiple real experiments on a global e-commerce platform. The sequence of checkpoints matters because adaptive stopping depends on evidence available during an experiment. The dataset’s design also reflects a discussion of what data common statistical tests require.

The paper demonstrates the resource using sequential and Bayesian hypothesis tests, including learning relevant parameters for each approach. These examples show how the dataset can support investigation of stopping decisions that could enable faster deployment of improvements or rollback of degrading changes. The contribution brings together a map of existing resources, a missing kind of public data, and concrete demonstrations of its use.
neurips-2021-datasets-for-online-control.tldr: A survey and new dataset of daily experiment metrics support research on adaptive stopping in online controlled experiments.

paragraphs: Protein engineering needs models that connect a protein’s sequence with properties relevant to a desired application. This relationship is often called a fitness landscape. FLIP introduces a benchmark focused on evaluating that relationship, addressing a gap between established protein structure or function benchmarks and the evaluation needs of protein engineering.

The benchmark combines curated data splits, baseline methods, and metrics designed to probe generalization in engineering-relevant conditions. These include learning from limited data and extrapolating beyond the examples available during training. This setup makes the evaluation conditions part of the contribution: the benchmark asks how representations support prediction under circumstances that matter for designing proteins.

FLIP includes experimental measurements involving adeno-associated virus stability for gene therapy, protein domain B1 stability and immunoglobulin binding, and thermostability across multiple protein families. The authors provide a standard data format and freely accessible scripts to support use and expansion. The result is a shared resource for comparing protein representations across several experimentally measured properties and generalization settings.
neurips-2021-flip-benchmark-tasks-in-fit.tldr: FLIP benchmarks protein-property prediction under limited-data and extrapolation conditions relevant to protein engineering.

paragraphs: Graph generation has applications such as network design and mobility synthesis, but available real-world datasets have been concentrated in a limited range of areas. GraphGT broadens the resources available for studying graph generation and transformation. Its collection contains 36 datasets spanning nine domains across six subjects.

The authors review and classify the datasets by research task, graph type, and application domain. They also process the source data to fit a unified framework for generation and transformation. This organization matters because a broad collection becomes more useful when researchers can understand its task structure and work with the data through consistent procedures.

GraphGT includes a pipeline for loading data, setting up experiments, and evaluating models, together with access through a Python library. The authors compare popular generative models on 16 generation datasets and 17 transformation datasets. These experiments demonstrate the collection’s ability to distinguish model capabilities and drawbacks, making it a common resource for evaluating methods across a wider range of graph problems.
neurips-2021-graphgt-machine-learning-da.tldr: GraphGT unifies diverse graph datasets and evaluation tools for comparing graph generation and transformation methods.

paragraphs: Training a robot control policy through reinforcement learning involves repeated interaction between a physics simulator and a learning system. Isaac Gym places both physics simulation and neural-network policy training on the GPU. The platform is intended to support a wide variety of robotics tasks through this integrated arrangement.

Its central implementation choice is direct communication between physics buffers and PyTorch tensors. Simulation data can therefore reach the learning system without passing through the CPU bottlenecks described in the paper. Keeping both parts of the training process on the same kind of processor makes this data path central to the platform’s performance.

For complex robotics tasks, the authors report training-time improvements of two to three orders of magnitude on a single GPU compared with conventional training that combines a CPU-based simulator with GPU neural networks. This is a claim about faster training in the reported comparison. The released simulator, benchmark, and environments provide resources for using and examining this GPU-based approach to robot learning.
neurips-2021-isaac-gym-high-performance-.tldr: Isaac Gym keeps physics simulation and policy training on the GPU, reporting training speedups of two to three orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Text-adventure games present worlds through language while revealing only part of the environment at any moment. An agent may need to keep track of hundreds of locations, characters, and objects during a long puzzle or quest. This paper introduces data for learning structured world models that can serve as memory in those settings.

The dataset connects natural-language observations to knowledge graphs representing the world state as a map. It also provides natural-language actions guaranteed to change the particular state associated with an example. Together, these targets support studying how an agent translates textual observations into structured information and identifies actions that affect its environment.

The training collection contains 24,198 mappings from 27 games across multiple genres, with 7,836 held-out instances from nine additional games for testing. The authors supply rule-based, question-answering, and sequence-learning baselines, along with analysis of the tasks. The resulting resource makes world-model construction and state-changing action prediction concrete learning problems grounded in interactive narratives.
neurips-2021-modeling-worlds-in-text-f46.tldr: A text-adventure dataset links observations to knowledge graphs and state-changing actions for learning structured world models.

paragraphs: Native Chinese Reader evaluates machine reading comprehension using material intended to assess the language proficiency of native Chinese high-school students. The authors collect questions from Chinese-course examinations, creating a dataset with longer passages and a broader range of writing styles than existing resources centered on short modern-Chinese contexts or particular domains.

The dataset contains 8,390 documents averaging 1,024 characters and 20,477 questions. Its coverage includes modern prose, classical literature, and classical poetry. Answering the questions requires reasoning and common sense as well as comprehension of the passages, giving the benchmark several interacting sources of difficulty.

The authors implement baselines using popular Chinese pretrained models and hold an online competition to examine available methods. The strongest model reaches 59% test accuracy, while human evaluation averages 79%. This comparison shows a substantial gap on the dataset between the tested systems and native speakers. NCR therefore provides a concrete setting for studying progress toward more demanding Chinese reading comprehension.
neurips-2021-native-chinese-reader-a-dat.tldr: NCR tests reasoning over long modern and classical Chinese passages, revealing a substantial model–human accuracy gap.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using records generated by a different policy. The paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating these estimates with realistic, reproducible public data. It introduces the Open Bandit Dataset, collected on the large fashion e-commerce platform ZOZOTOWN.

The key feature is that the resource includes multiple logged datasets produced by running different policies on the same platform. This gives researchers a shared basis for experimentally comparing off-policy estimators. The collection directly addresses the authors’ concern that the absence of suitable public real-world data had made studies difficult to reproduce and disconnected from realistic settings.

The accompanying Open Bandit Pipeline is Python software that standardizes and simplifies implementation of batch bandit algorithms and off-policy evaluation. The authors use the data and software for extensive experiments with existing estimators, reporting that the results reveal important challenges and research opportunities. Together, the resources support more transparent comparisons through shared observations, implementation tools, and benchmark experiments.
neurips-2021-open-bandit-dataset-and-pip.tldr: Open Bandit combines real e-commerce logs from multiple policies with shared software for reproducible off-policy evaluation.

paragraphs: PROCAT studies the problem of turning a set of items into an organized sequence. Its examples are professionally designed e-commerce catalogues, where individual product offers are arranged into complementary sections. This makes the task involve both ordering the items and capturing the larger structure of the catalogue.

The dataset contains more than 1.5 million set items collected across four years. It provides raw text and processed features that include information about relative visual placement. The task includes rare and previously unseen items, varying sequence lengths, and catalogues with different internal structures, all of which contribute to the difficulty of predicting an appropriate arrangement.

The authors also define a benchmark task and report baseline experiments using several architectures that jointly encode sets and learn permutations. These resources address the scarcity of datasets for complex set-to-sequence prediction. The expertly designed catalogues provide concrete examples through which researchers can study how models learn ordering, implicit grouping, and structure together.
neurips-2021-procat-product-catalogue-da.tldr: PROCAT uses expertly arranged product catalogues to benchmark learning how to group and order sets into structured sequences.

paragraphs: Conditional average treatment effect estimation studies how treatment effects differ across groups characterized by observed information. Many machine-learning methods for this problem have been tested on only a narrow set of semi-synthetic datasets. This paper examines what those evaluations establish, focusing particularly on the widely used IHDP benchmark.

The authors argue that semi-synthetic datasets do not necessarily preserve the properties of real data and can systematically favor some algorithms. Consequently, a strong result may partly reflect how a benchmark was constructed. This matters for interpreting empirical rankings because success under a particular generated setup does not by itself establish suitability across real applications.

The paper also questions whether commonly used metrics cover the purposes for which treatment-effect estimates are needed. The authors argue that current metrics address only a small subset of possible uses and discuss alternatives relevant to personalized medicine. Alongside alternative datasets, these considerations frame evaluation as a choice that should reflect both the data setting and the intended application.
neurips-2021-really-doing-great-at-estim.tldr: The paper shows how semi-synthetic benchmark design and narrow metrics can distort comparisons of treatment-effect estimators.

paragraphs: Understanding an instruction requires combining words into references to entities, relationships, and actions. This paper examines whether a benchmark actually demands that kind of compositional interpretation. The authors show that the constrained design of gSCAN allows successful performance without using many details of its instructions and scenarios.

ReaSCAN builds on gSCAN while requiring models to interpret language compositionally and reason about entities and their relations. Its purpose is to make the relevant linguistic structure necessary for solving the benchmark tasks. This addresses the evaluation problem identified in the earlier dataset: task success could otherwise give an overly favorable impression of compositional understanding.

The authors evaluate a multimodal baseline and a leading graph convolutional model. Both find ReaSCAN substantially harder than gSCAN. These experiments support the claim that the revised benchmark presents a stronger challenge for the two tested architectures. The authors suggest that it can help researchers investigate compositional generalization and reasoning by tying successful language grounding more closely to the intended abilities.
neurips-2021-reascan-compositional-reaso.tldr: ReaSCAN strengthens language-grounding evaluation by requiring compositional reasoning that gSCAN can leave unnecessary.

paragraphs: Describing a scientific table can require calculations and interpretation of numerical relationships. SciGen introduces a dataset of scientific tables and associated descriptions to evaluate text generation that involves this arithmetic reasoning. Its mostly numerical tables create a structured input setting in which producing fluent text also demands reasoning about values.

The core dataset, including the test portion, uses annotations supplied by an author of each corresponding scientific article. Because this expert involvement is difficult to scale, the researchers also develop a pipeline that automatically extracts high-quality table-description pairs from article LaTeX sources. The approach combines an expert-annotated core with a way to obtain additional training material.

The authors evaluate leading data-to-text systems using common metrics and human judgments. Adding high-quality unsupervised training data improves correctness and reduces hallucination in generated descriptions. However, the evaluated models remain severely limited on the task. These findings show both the value of additional suitable training data and the continuing difficulty of generating accurate descriptions that depend on arithmetic reasoning.
neurips-2021-scigen-a-dataset-for-reason.tldr: SciGen tests arithmetic reasoning in scientific table descriptions, where additional training data helps but tested models remain severely limited.

paragraphs: Modeling sequences of medical decisions poses challenges that standard machine-learning tasks may not capture well. The authors point to limited public access to realistic data, the offline nature of the problem, and the variety and complexity of human behavior. Medkit-Learn provides a benchmark suite designed specifically around these medical decision-modeling needs.

The suite is a public Python package offering access to high-fidelity synthetic medical data. Its generating process separates the policy governing decisions from the dynamics of the environment. This separation allows customization of these components, creating a way to examine algorithm behavior under controlled changes in the simulated medical setting.

The main contribution is a standardized but configurable environment for comparing algorithms and investigating robustness to healthcare-specific challenges. The synthetic data and adjustable generating process support systematic evaluation where suitable public data are scarce. The paper positions this capability as a foundation for understanding clinical decision-making behavior, with improved patient outcomes serving as the broader motivation for the research.
neurips-2021-the-medkit-learn-ing-enviro.tldr: Medkit-Learn offers configurable synthetic medical data for benchmarking sequential decision models and their robustness.

paragraphs: Studying animal social behavior requires precise measurements of how interacting animals move in three dimensions. Comparing methods for estimating those poses has been difficult without shared training and evaluation data. PAIR-R24M addresses that need with a large collection of recorded interactions between pairs of laboratory rats.

The dataset contains 24.3 million RGB video frames together with three-dimensional motion-capture ground truth. It covers 18 distinct rat pairs and 24 viewpoints. The authors additionally annotate 11 behaviors and three interaction categories, providing a basis for evaluating methods on rare but difficult behaviors as well as the broader collection.

To establish a markerless pose-estimation baseline, the authors extend DANNCE, an existing network for freely behaving laboratory animals, to handle multiple animals. The dataset and baseline together create a shared starting point for studying multi-animal tracking. The anticipated scientific benefit is better measurement of social interactions, which could support future investigation of their biological and neural basis.
neurips-2021-the-pair-r24m-dataset-for-m.tldr: PAIR-R24M pairs rat-interaction videos with 3D motion capture to benchmark multi-animal pose estimation.

paragraphs: The People’s Speech provides a large supervised dataset for conversational English speech recognition. The paper describes a collection of 31,400 hours that is free to download and licensed under CC-BY-SA for academic and commercial use. Its contribution combines the scale of the audio collection with explicit terms for using the resource.

The authors gather appropriately licensed online audio that already has transcriptions. They describe this collection process and release the collection system under the Apache 2.0 license. Providing both the data and the software makes the resource useful at two levels: researchers can train with the assembled material and inspect the system used to collect it.

A model trained on the dataset achieves a 32.17% word error rate on LibriSpeech’s test-clean set, providing a concrete reported result for its use in speech recognition. The paper also discusses legal and ethical issues involved in assembling a large corpus and describes plans for continued maintenance with MLCommons sponsorship. These elements make dataset stewardship part of the contribution alongside collection and evaluation.
neurips-2021-the-peoples-speech-a-large-.tldr: The People’s Speech releases 31,400 hours of licensed English speech data and the software used to collect it.

paragraphs: Weak supervision creates training labels by combining sources that may be noisy, helping reduce the need for manual annotation. Comparing these methods is difficult when studies use private datasets, different labeling sources, or inconsistent evaluation procedures. WRENCH introduces a shared benchmark platform to make these comparisons more standardized.

The platform contains 22 real-world datasets covering classification and sequence tagging, together with real, synthetic, and procedurally generated supervision sources. It also provides an extensible modular framework and implementations of popular methods. This matters because even datasets with identical names and underlying examples can produce different evaluations when their labels or supervision sources differ.

The authors use WRENCH to compare more than 120 method variants, demonstrating its use for extensive evaluation within a common framework. The contribution is a coordinated collection of data, supervision sources, implementations, and evaluation tools. By making those experimental ingredients explicit, WRENCH addresses hidden variation that can otherwise make weak-supervision results difficult to interpret across studies.
neurips-2021-wrench-a-comprehensive-benc.tldr: WRENCH standardizes weak-supervision evaluation with 22 datasets, varied supervision sources, and a modular benchmarking framework.
